source.title: [Interim research report] Taking features out of superposition with sparse autoencoders

record.tranche_reason: The post discusses superposition and polysemanticity, but its experiments assess sparse-autoencoder feature recovery, not neuron-pole job counts, explanations on held-out activations, or the other specified versions.
record.gate_note: The reported SAE results concern recovery and consistency of learned feature directions, a related but different construct from the versions' claims about neuron poles or neuron-based explanations. SAE dead-neuron and loss-stickiness diagnostics are not results about model neurons' jobs or explanation fidelity.
record.test_reason: The post trains sparse autoencoders on synthetic data and a small LM's MLP activations and measures dictionary recovery (MMCS). It reports no share of single-job neurons, no re-analysis of canonical polysemantic neurons, no interpretable-neuron share across tools or architectures, no neuron-based attribution graphs, and no held-out explanation scoring. It assumes superposition as motivation but does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also give very weak, tentative evidence that the 256-dim model may hold over 100,000 features in superposition. They suggest sparse coding may be very costly to scale and that building models without superposition looks attractive. In a later comment the author says the LM results were likely undertrained.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains sparse autoencoders on toy data and MLP activations and evaluates dictionary feature recovery; it does not use the neuron-pole audit or explanation-testing methods in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: In the toy experiments, the useful L1 penalty range depends on dictionary size; the authors report that larger dictionaries require larger L1 penalties. The small-language-model diagnostics differ from the toy-data results.

fits_no_version.finding: Single-layer L1 sparse autoencoders recover ground-truth directions in synthetic superposed data across a broad L1 range (~0.03–0.3) and 1–8x dictionary sizes. On a 31M LM's MLP, dictionaries of different sizes reach at most ~0.4 MMCS with each other, and no dead neurons appear up to 102400 features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE dictionary learning recovers known features in toy superposition data, but its feature consistency on real LM MLP activations was low and inconclusive in this early setup.

record.code_released: no; the post says code would be included in a final research report, but none is included here
record.peer_reviewed: Alignment Forum post; peer-review status not stated
record.problems: The authors describe the language-model results as preliminary and uncertain. They note possible insufficient dictionary size, undertraining, noise, and mismatches between toy and real activations; they also state that toy-data recovery assumptions may not transfer to the language model.
record.rows_left_out: The post also reports SAE dead-neuron counts, loss-stickiness diagnostics, and other hyperparameter-search plots. These concern SAE behavior and hyperparameter selection rather than neuron-pole jobs or explanation fidelity, so they were not recorded as rows.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles.
No cross-model or cross-scale neuron job shares.
No analysis of InceptionV1 or of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No interpretable-neuron share measured across tools or architectures.
No neuron-based attribution graphs and no replacement-model comparison.
No test of explanations against held-out activations.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: This is an Alignment Forum interim report and the precursor to SAE work; it assumes superposition rather than testing neuron monosemanticity. Its 'dead neurons' are SAE hidden units, not model neurons. Its rows record the study's own method performance, so no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B or count neuron poles by number of jobs.
Does not compare neuron-pole job shares across models, architectures, or scales.
Does not analyze InceptionV1's cat-and-car neuron or recursive generalization.
Does not estimate interpretable-neuron shares across architectures or tools.
Does not build attribution graphs or test whether model neurons suffice as circuit units.
Does not test explanations against activations beyond those they were written from.
Does not score neuron explanations by predicting activations on new text.

rows.subject: toy data
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean max cosine similarity between sparse-autoencoder dictionary elements and known ground-truth features while varying the L1 penalty.

conditions.value: 512, equal to the number of ground-truth features
sweep; acceptable range reported as around 0.03 to around 0.3

rows.measure: Mean max cosine similarity (MMCS), as a measure of ground-truth feature recovery
rows.baseline: Ground-truth feature directions; no numeric baseline stated
rows.value: The text reports high MMCS in a broad range of L1 penalties, around 0.03 to around 0.3; exact values are shown in Figure 1.
rows.locator: Experimental results, “The L1 penalty coefficient needs to be just right”; Figure 1
rows.note: The post reports that the learned dictionary recovers ground-truth features in this synthetic setting. This does not measure neuron-pole job counts.
rows.check: Synthetic-data SAE recovery (MMCS vs L1). This is method validation on toy data, not a measure of model neurons' jobs; the state relative to the claim versions cannot be determined.

rows.subject: toy data
rows.operation_detail: Measured MMCS while varying learned dictionary size.

conditions.value: between 1 and 8 times the ground-truth dictionary size

rows.measure: Mean max cosine similarity (MMCS), as a measure of ground-truth feature recovery
rows.baseline: Ground-truth feature directions; no numeric baseline stated
rows.value: The text says the ground-truth features can be almost completely recovered with dictionaries between 1 and 8 times the ground-truth dictionary size, with MMCS decreasing only slowly as size increases.
rows.locator: Experimental results, “We need more learned features than ground truth features”; Figure 2
rows.note: This is synthetic-data feature recovery, not a result about the share of interpretable model neurons.
rows.check: Synthetic-data SAE recovery vs dictionary size. This is the study's own method performance, not a neuron-level result; no version bears on it.

rows.subject: small language model
rows.stage_stated: trained by the authors on the Wikipedia subset of the Pile
rows.operation_detail: Compared sparse-autoencoder dictionaries of different sizes using mean max cosine similarity.

conditions.value: layer 1, described as the second MLP layer

rows.measure: MMCS between a dictionary and larger dictionaries
rows.value: The MMCS between dictionaries never exceeds approximately 0.4; the text says the optimal dictionary size is unclear.
rows.locator: Experimental results, “Mean max cosine similarity between a dictionary and those larger than it”; Figure 13
rows.note: The authors describe the outcome as tentative and say dictionaries of different sizes often learn quite different features. It does not measure neuron-pole jobs.
rows.check: Dictionary-to-dictionary MMCS (max ~0.4) on a 31M LM's layer-1 MLP is an SAE consistency diagnostic, not a neuron interpretability share.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
